questions.stem: During colonoscopy, a patient opens her eyes and follows a command only after repeated trapezius squeeze. Which sedation level best fits?
questions.explanation: Purposeful response only after repeated or painful stimulation defines deep sedation. Moderate sedation responds to voice or light touch; general anesthesia is unarousable even to pain.

questions.stem: During propofol sedation, painful stimulation produces only reflex withdrawal and a jaw thrust is required to maintain airflow. How should the depth be interpreted?
options: The patient has progressed beyond deep sedation into general anesthesia
The patient remains deeply sedated because any movement to pain is purposeful
The patient is moderately sedated because spontaneous breathing persists
The patient is minimally sedated because withdrawal is present
questions.explanation: Purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation defines deep sedation; reflex withdrawal alone does not count, so he may be at GA. Moderate sedation requires purposeful response to voice or light touch, and spontaneous breathing does not define the level.

questions.stem: As propofol depth increases from moderate sedation through general anesthesia, which physiologic domain is generally preserved the longest on the ASA continuum?
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular function is usually maintained through deep sedation and is described as possibly impaired only at GA. Ventilation becomes possibly inadequate earlier, at deep sedation, and the airway may need intervention there.

questions.stem: Among minimal, moderate, and deep sedation, at which level does airway intervention first become potentially necessary?
questions.explanation: Airway intervention "may be required" first appears at deep sedation (patient C). Moderate sedation (patient B) requires no intervention, minimal sedation (A) leaves the airway unaffected, and at GA intervention is often required.

questions.stem: After a small midazolam dose, a patient remains conversational but has impaired coordination. Which level best fits?
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation allows impaired cognition and coordination while ventilation and cardiovascular function remain unaffected. Impaired coordination alone does not move the patient to moderate sedation.

questions.stem: Oral midazolam is intended only for MRI anxiolysis. Which change most clearly indicates progression beyond minimal sedation?
options: Loss of a normal response to verbal interaction
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation aims to reduce anxiety while keeping normal response to voice and intact protective reflexes. Losing normal conversational response means she has moved to moderate sedation. Reduced anxiety, normal breathing, and some recall are all consistent with the goal.

questions.stem: During propofol sedation, the patient becomes intermittently apneic and is unarousable even to painful stimulation. Which classification best fits?
options: General anesthesia with frequently inadequate ventilation
Deep sedation with reliably adequate ventilation
Moderate sedation with possible airway intervention
questions.explanation: "Frequently inadequate" ventilation belongs to GA, which also fits his lack of purposeful response to pain. Deep sedation is "may be inadequate," moderate is "adequate," and minimal is "unaffected."

questions.stem: Moderate sedation is planned for a patient with OSA. What level of rescue capability must the sedation provider possess?
options: Ability to rescue from deep sedation
Ability to rescue only from the intended moderate level
Ability to rescue only from minimal sedation
Reliance on a separate code team for deeper sedation
questions.explanation: Because depth moves along a continuum, a provider must be able to rescue a patient from the next deeper level. Planning only for the intended level, or relying on others for rescue, misses that principle.

questions.stem: During intended moderate sedation, sustained jaw thrust becomes necessary to maintain airflow and the patient responds only to painful stimulation. What should the provider recognize?
options: The patient is deeply sedated and rescue capability for progression to general anesthesia must be immediately available
Routine tracheal intubation is mandatory for every deeply sedated patient
The patient remains moderately sedated because spontaneous ventilation continues
Jaw thrust alone proves general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Needing jaw thrust puts the patient at deep sedation, one step from GA, so the provider must be able to rescue from GA. That does not mean every deeply sedated patient is intubated.

questions.stem: A patient is conversational early in colonoscopy but later snores and obstructs after the stimulating portion ends despite no additional drug. Which principle best explains this?
options: Sedation depth reflects both drug effect and changing procedural stimulation
Moderate sedation requires continuous core-temperature monitoring
Cardiovascular function must be impaired before airway obstruction occurs
Propofol begins accumulating only after 20 minutes
questions.explanation: Depth moves as boluses peak and stimulation rises and falls, which is why moderate sedation requires continuous reassessment. Patients at moderate depth can still respond, and cardiovascular function is usually maintained.

questions.stem: Patient A responds purposefully to voice without airway support. Patient B responds only to painful stimulation and requires jaw thrust. Which comparison is correct?
options: A is moderately sedated; B is deeply sedated
A is minimally sedated; B is moderately sedated
A is deeply sedated; B is under general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation means purposeful response to voice or light touch with no airway intervention. Deep sedation means purposeful response only after repeated or painful stimulation, with airway intervention possibly required.

questions.stem: A patient intended for moderate sedation now follows a command only after firm sternal rub. What is the best interpretation?
options: The patient has progressed to deep sedation and airway/ventilation readiness should increase
The patient remains moderately sedated because a response is present
The patient is under general anesthesia because painful stimulation was needed
The patient is minimally sedated because a command was followed
questions.explanation: Purposeful response only after painful stimulation places him in deep sedation, beyond the intended level. That change should trigger closer airway and ventilation monitoring and a readiness to support.

questions.stem: A drowsy patient opens her eyes and follows a command when her name is spoken with light touch. Which level is present?
questions.explanation: Purposeful response to verbal or light tactile stimulation is moderate ("conscious") sedation. Closed eyes do not change the level; the type of stimulus needed and the response do.

questions.stem: As propofol depth increases, cough to pooled secretions weakens and disappears. Which principle does this illustrate?
options: Protective airway reflexes become progressively less reliable as depth increases
Airway reflexes remain intact until general anesthesia begins
Airway reflexes disappear during minimal sedation
Protective reflexes strengthen as sedation deepens
questions.explanation: The ASA continuum describes progressive impairment of responsiveness, protective reflexes, ventilation, and cardiovascular function as depth increases. The loss is gradual rather than a single cutoff.

questions.stem: Small doses of midazolam and fentanyl together produce much greater hypoventilation than either dose would be expected to cause alone. Which principle best explains this?
options: Opioid-induced chest-wall rigidity at routine low dose
questions.explanation: Benzodiazepines and opioids depress ventilation synergistically, so their combined effect is greater than the sum of each. Low-dose fentanyl rarely causes rigidity, and an allergy would not present this way.

questions.stem: A patient responds purposefully only after painful stimulation and requires jaw thrust while BP remains stable. Which TWO statements are correct? (Select 2)
options: The patient is not easily aroused
No airway intervention should be necessary
Cardiovascular function is expected to be severely impaired
The patient has a normal response to verbal commands
The patient meets the definition of moderate sedation
questions.explanation: She is at deep sedation: not easily aroused, with ventilation possibly impaired and airway help needed. Cardiovascular function is usually maintained at this level, as her stable BP shows.

questions.stem: Which FOUR features are expected during moderate sedation? (Select 4)
options: Purposeful response to verbal or light tactile stimulation
Spontaneous ventilation is expected to remain adequate
Airway intervention is not routinely required
questions.explanation: At moderate sedation, patients respond purposefully to verbal or light tactile stimulation, spontaneous ventilation is expected to remain adequate, airway intervention is not routinely required, and cardiovascular function is usually maintained. Monitoring requirements depend on the clinical setting and applicable standards; capnography is addressed separately.

questions.stem: During propofol for EGD, the patient no longer responds purposefully even to painful stimulation and ventilation becomes inadequate. What should the provider recognize?
options: The patient has crossed into general anesthesia and requires rescue of airway/ventilation as needed
This is ideal moderate sedation for upper endoscopy
Propofol has supplied sufficient analgesia for the procedure
Loss of responsiveness does not change airway risk
questions.explanation: No purposeful response even to painful stimulation is consistent with general anesthesia on the ASA continuum, especially when ventilation is inadequate. Propofol supplies hypnosis but little analgesia, so airway and ventilatory rescue must take priority.

questions.stem: A minimally sedated patient remains normally conversational but develops a large blood-pressure decrease. How should this be interpreted?
options: The hypotension is not explained by the expected physiology of minimal sedation and another cause should be sought
Cardiovascular depression is expected at minimal sedation
The patient must have progressed to deep sedation solely because BP fell
Minimal sedation routinely produces major vasodilation
questions.explanation: At minimal sedation, cardiovascular function is unaffected. A 20% BP drop at this level should prompt a search for another cause, such as hypovolemia or vagal response.

questions.stem: Which airway-intervention descriptor correctly matches the ASA sedation continuum?
options: Moderate sedation: intervention may be required
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation leaves the airway unaffected, moderate requires no intervention, deep may require it, and GA often requires it.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, which physiologic function is still described as usually maintained?
questions.explanation: At deep sedation, cardiovascular function is usually maintained, while ventilation may be inadequate and the airway may need intervention. Normal response to voice belongs to minimal sedation.

questions.stem: Only minimal sedation is planned. From which next-deeper level must the provider still be able to rescue the patient?
questions.explanation: You must be able to rescue a patient from the level beyond your target. For planned minimal sedation, that is moderate sedation.

questions.stem: A patient is unarousable even to painful stimulation and hypoventilating. Which responsiveness category applies?
questions.explanation: Being unarousable even to painful stimulation defines GA. Purposeful response after repeated or painful stimulation is deep sedation.

questions.stem: Late in a long procedure, a moderately sedated patient becomes restless as stimulation increases. Why is simply giving repeated sedative boluses risky?
options: When stimulation falls, accumulated drug effect may push the patient into deeper-than-intended sedation
Restlessness proves the patient cannot become oversedated
Additional sedative will necessarily improve ventilation
The main risk is hypertension rather than airway/ventilatory depression
questions.explanation: Long cases bring restlessness and disinhibition, which prompt more drug and raise the chance of deeper-than-intended sedation with an unsecured airway. Disinhibition can itself be a sign of oversedation.

questions.stem: Repeated painful stimulation produces only reflex withdrawal without purposeful response. Which depth is most consistent with the ASA continuum?
questions.explanation: Reflex withdrawal is not a purposeful response. Deep sedation requires purposeful response to repeated or painful stimulation, so a reflex-only response places her at GA.

questions.stem: "Conscious sedation" corresponds to which ASA level and expected airway state?
options: Moderate sedation; airway intervention is not routinely required
Minimal sedation; airway intervention may be required
Deep sedation; airway intervention is never required
questions.explanation: Conscious sedation is synonymous with moderate sedation/analgesia, which requires no airway intervention. If the patient needs airway support, he has moved beyond the intended level.

questions.stem: Repeated equal propofol boluses eventually produce obstruction after initially producing only moderate sedation. Which principle best explains this?
options: Sedation is a continuum, and cumulative drug effect can move a patient across levels
Each equal bolus produces a fixed, reproducible depth
Propofol cannot deepen sedation without a change in stimulus
Sedation level depends only on the drug selected, not dose or patient response
questions.explanation: Sedation is a continuum, so cumulative dosing and changing stimulation can shift a patient across levels without warning.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, RR falls to 7/min with shallow breaths. How should this be interpreted?
options: Ventilation may be inadequate at this depth and should be assessed/supported
Ventilation is expected to remain unaffected during deep sedation
Respiratory depression occurs only during general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Spontaneous ventilation "may be inadequate" at deep sedation. It is an anticipated risk requiring assessment and support, not proof of GA.

questions.stem: A patient progresses from normal response to voice, to purposeful response only when directly stimulated, to purposeful response only after painful stimulation, then to no purposeful response. Which sequence fits?
questions.explanation: The ASA continuum runs minimal (anxiolysis), moderate (conscious sedation), deep, and general anesthesia.

questions.stem: A patient intended for moderate sedation later follows commands only after repeated stimulation. What should the provider do?
options: Recognize progression to deep sedation, hold further dosing, and reassess airway/ventilation
Continue dosing because any command-following defines moderate sedation
Classify the patient as minimally sedated
Assume general anesthesia and intubate regardless of ventilation
questions.explanation: Response only after repeated stimulation suggests deep sedation. Hold further sedative, reassess ventilation, and be ready to support the airway.

questions.stem: Which FOUR features characterize general anesthesia on the ASA sedation continuum? (Select 4)
options: Purposeful response after repeated painful stimulation
questions.explanation: At GA, patients are unarousable, need airway intervention often, have frequently inadequate ventilation, and may have impaired cardiovascular function.

questions.stem: Patient A converses normally after midazolam. Patient B gives a purposeful answer only when directly addressed. Which comparison is most accurate?
options: A is minimally sedated; B is moderately sedated
A is moderately sedated; B is deeply sedated
questions.explanation: Minimal sedation keeps a normal response to voice; moderate sedation keeps a purposeful but diminished response.

questions.stem: During GI sedation, external abdominal pressure is applied while protective airway reflexes are depressed. Which hazard is increased?
options: Regurgitation and aspiration of gastric contents
questions.explanation: The handwritten note flags aspiration from pushing on the stomach in the GI suite. Abdominal pressure during colonoscopy can push gastric contents up in a patient with impaired reflexes.

questions.stem: A patient appears lighter during intense procedural stimulation, receives additional sedative, then obstructs when stimulation abruptly stops. What caused the overshoot?
options: Drug dosing was titrated to transient stimulation rather than anticipating the subsequent fall in stimulus
Sedation depth is independent of procedural stimulation
The airway obstruction proves an allergic reaction
questions.explanation: Titration must match changing procedural stimulus. Intense stimulation often lightens the patient and prompts extra dosing, and depth can overshoot once the stimulus ends.

questions.stem: Which finding most clearly marks progression from minimal to moderate sedation?
options: Purposeful but diminished response to verbal stimulation rather than a normal conversational response
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation is purposeful but not normal response to voice. Relaxation, normal breathing, and stable BP all fit minimal sedation as well.

questions.stem: A patient with EF 25% becomes hypotensive during deep sedation. Why does the continuum's phrase "cardiovascular function usually maintained" not exclude sedation as a contributor?
options: Population-level descriptors do not guarantee hemodynamic tolerance in a patient with limited reserve
Cardiovascular function is always severely impaired during deep sedation
Deep sedation cannot affect vascular tone
Hypotension proves the patient is minimally sedated
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular function is usually maintained at deep sedation, but patients with limited reserve can still become unstable. Treat the hypotension and check the patient first.

questions.stem: A synchronized cardioversion requires immobility for a brief but intensely painful stimulus. Which sedation target is commonly appropriate when full rescue capability is present?
options: Routine moderate sedation regardless of response
No sedation because the stimulus is brief
questions.explanation: Cardioversion is intensely stimulating but very short, so it is usually done under brief deep sedation. The other procedures are commonly done at minimal to moderate depth in selected patients.

questions.stem: A patient moves from purposeful response to voice, to purposeful response only after repeated/painful stimulation, to no purposeful response. Which transition occurred?
options: Moderate sedation → deep sedation → general anesthesia
Deep sedation → moderate sedation → general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Answering to her name is moderate; responding only to repeated stimulation is deep; no purposeful response is GA.

questions.stem: For planned anxiolysis, which combination should be preserved?
options: Normal response to verbal stimulation with an unaffected airway
Purposeful response only to painful stimulation with possible airway intervention
No response to pain with frequent ventilatory inadequacy
Diminished response to voice with airway intervention often required
questions.explanation: Anxiolysis is minimal sedation, with normal response to verbal stimulation and an unaffected airway.

questions.stem: A patient initially pushes away painful stimulation purposefully but, after another propofol bolus, has no purposeful response to pain. Which transition occurred?
options: No change because spontaneous breathing may persist
questions.explanation: Loss of purposeful response to painful stimulation marks the move from deep sedation to GA.

questions.stem: During intended deep sedation, the patient becomes unresponsive to pain with severe hypoventilation. What is the correct response?
options: Recognize general anesthesia and rescue airway/ventilation
Label this moderate sedation and observe
questions.explanation: Unresponsiveness to painful stimulation with inadequate ventilation is general anesthesia. Anyone providing deep sedation must be able to rescue a patient who enters GA.

questions.stem: A quiet patient on propofol has regular respirations and SpO2 99% on oxygen. What is the best way to determine actual sedation depth?
options: Assess response to appropriate verbal/tactile or painful stimulation
Infer depth from propofol dose alone
questions.explanation: Depth is defined by response to stimulation. Without stimulating, you cannot tell moderate from deep sedation or GA; breathing pattern, SpO2, and dose do not define the level.

questions.stem: During moderate sedation with supplemental oxygen, which monitor detects hypoventilation most directly and earlier than pulse oximetry?
questions.explanation: Moderate sedation should keep ventilation adequate, but capnography confirms it. SpO2 lags on supplemental oxygen, and chest movement can occur with obstruction.

questions.stem: A patient still responds purposefully to voice, but RR falls to 6/min and ETCO2 rises. What should drive immediate management?
options: The ventilatory failure should be treated despite the preserved responsiveness
No action is needed because responsiveness defines moderate sedation
The patient must be under general anesthesia
questions.explanation: Depth labels are based on responsiveness, but ventilation can fail at any depth, especially with opioids. Treat the hypoventilation first.

questions.stem: Which ASA descriptor is unchanged when moving from moderate to deep sedation?
questions.explanation: Cardiovascular function is usually maintained at both moderate and deep sedation. Responsiveness, airway, and ventilation all worsen.

questions.stem: Brief deep sedation is planned for cardioversion. Which preparation is required before drug administration?
options: Immediate capability and equipment to rescue from general anesthesia, including advanced airway management
Only a nasal cannula because the procedure is brief
Only an oral airway and suction
No advanced rescue preparation if spontaneous ventilation is expected
questions.explanation: Deep sedation requires readiness to rescue from GA, which means full airway equipment including laryngoscopy and advanced airways.

questions.stem: A patient has intermittent apnea but still purposefully pushes away painful stimulation. Which classification best fits?
options: Moderate sedation with reliably adequate ventilation
General anesthesia because any apnea defines GA
questions.explanation: Purposeful response only to painful stimulation is consistent with deep sedation, where ventilation may be inadequate. Intermittent apnea requires immediate ventilatory assessment/support even though apnea alone does not define general anesthesia.

questions.stem: Responsiveness, airway reflexes, ventilation, and eventually cardiovascular function progressively decline as drug effect increases. Which model does this describe?
options: A fixed classification determined by drug name
Four physiologically isolated states with sharp boundaries
questions.explanation: The ASA describes sedation as a continuum where responsiveness, airway, ventilation, and cardiovascular function progressively decline.

questions.stem: A calm patient after oral midazolam responds normally to conversation and breathes unaided. Which airway descriptor best fits?
options: Airway is protected only by an endotracheal tube
questions.explanation: Only minimal sedation describes the airway as unaffected. Moderate sedation is "no intervention required," which is not the same as unaffected.

questions.stem: A patient intended for moderate sedation now responds purposefully only to painful stimulation. What is the first priority?
options: Recognize deep sedation, stop further dosing, and assess/support airway and ventilation
Proceed unchanged because purposeful response persists
Intubate automatically even if ventilation is adequate
questions.explanation: She has moved into deep sedation. The first step is assessing airway and ventilation and holding further drug while supporting as needed.

questions.stem: Before propofol sedation in a patient with a short neck and limited mouth opening, which question should drive planning?
options: Can I oxygenate, ventilate, and secure the airway if sedation becomes deeper than intended?
Will the patient remember the procedure?
Does the proceduralist prefer deep sedation?
questions.explanation: Every sedation plan starts with whether you can rescue the airway if depth overshoots. A difficult-looking airway makes that question the deciding factor in the plan.

questions.stem: Mallampati III is present. Which additional finding most increases concern about difficult rescue laryngoscopy?
questions.explanation: A short thyromental distance predicts difficult laryngoscopy and adds to Mallampati III. The other findings do not predict airway difficulty.

questions.stem: During LEMON assessment, mouth opening, mandibular space, and the position of the larynx are estimated with fingerbreadths. Which component is being used?
questions.explanation: LEMON stands for Look externally, Evaluate 3-3-2, Mallampati, Obstruction, Neck mobility. Fingerbreadth measurements belong to the 3-3-2 evaluation.

questions.stem: Only two fingerbreadths of mouth opening are present. Which rescue task is most directly compromised?
options: Insertion/manipulation of laryngoscopy and other oral airway devices
Mask seal around the nose and mouth
questions.explanation: The first "3" measures mouth opening; fewer than three fingerbreadths limits laryngoscope and device insertion. The second 3 measures the mandibular space, and the 2 measures larynx position.

questions.stem: Severe OSA with markedly enlarged tonsils most directly maps to which LEMON concern?
questions.explanation: O in LEMON is obstruction, which includes sleep apnea, enlarged tonsils, and tumors. Mallampati and neck mobility are assessed separately.

questions.stem: A patient reports prior difficult mask ventilation and difficult intubation during anesthesia. Why is this history especially important before sedation?
options: It predicts potentially difficult rescue if sedation progresses deeper than intended
It predicts a higher sedative requirement
It makes all procedural sedation contraindicated
questions.explanation: A history of difficult mask ventilation, difficult intubation, or OSA predicts difficulty rescuing the airway if sedation overshoots. It shapes drug choice, depth, and backup equipment.

questions.stem: When should oxygen delivery, suction, bag-mask ventilation, and advanced airway-rescue equipment be ready for planned moderate sedation?
options: Only when a difficult airway is predicted
questions.explanation: Oxygen and rescue equipment must be ready before any sedative, because depth can change quickly even in healthy patients.

questions.stem: A patient with symptomatic gastroparesis is scheduled for EGD under sedation. Why does this alter the risk-benefit assessment?
options: Delayed gastric emptying increases aspiration risk while sedation may impair protective airway reflexes without securing the airway
Sedatives increase gastric acid production enough to cause aspiration
Sedation itself completely stops gastric emptying
questions.explanation: Sedation impairs protective reflexes without securing the airway. Aspiration risk calls for caution and may push the plan toward GA, but it does not forbid sedation.

questions.stem: Which patient has the fewest patient-specific features requiring modification of a routine sedation plan?
options: A healthy ASA I adult with a normal airway examination
An older adult taking nightly clonazepam
A patient with cirrhosis and ascites
A patient with bulbar weakness and dysphagia
questions.explanation: Chronic benzodiazepine use, hepatic dysfunction, and neurologic disease affecting airway reflexes all require extra caution. A healthy ASA I with a normal airway does not.

questions.stem: A heavy alcohol user taking chronic alprazolam requires unusually high sedative doses, then becomes apneic after a small additional dose. Which principle best explains the unpredictability?
options: Tolerance can alter dose requirements, while combined sedatives can still abruptly produce profound respiratory depression
Tolerance eliminates the risk of oversedation
questions.explanation: Chronic benzodiazepine or alcohol exposure creates tolerance and an unpredictable response, so titrate carefully.

questions.stem: A patient with cirrhosis and advanced CKD remains sedated far longer than expected after midazolam. Which mechanism best explains the prolonged effect?
options: Impaired metabolism/clearance of drug and active metabolites
questions.explanation: Renal and hepatic dysfunction alter metabolism and clearance of sedatives and their active metabolites, prolonging effects.

questions.stem: Parkinson disease with prominent dysphagia most directly increases which sedation concern?
options: Impaired swallowing/airway protection with increased aspiration risk
questions.explanation: Parkinson's with dysphagia impairs swallowing and airway protection, raising aspiration and obstruction risk.

questions.stem: Which FOUR patients warrant added caution before procedural sedation? (Select 4)
options: An uncooperative patient unable to remain still
A healthy 30-year-old with a normal airway
A patient with isolated seasonal allergies
questions.explanation: Suspected sleep apnea, frailty, uncooperative behavior, and chronic opioid use all call for extra caution.

questions.stem: A full beard, small mandible, and facial trauma are identified before sedation. Which LEMON step captures these external predictors?
questions.explanation: Visible external features such as beards, a small mandible, and facial trauma fall under "look externally."

questions.stem: The lower incisors cannot protrude beyond the upper incisors. Which rescue function may be more difficult?
options: Mandibular advancement/jaw thrust and laryngoscopic tongue displacement
Obtaining a facemask seal solely because of dentition
questions.explanation: Limited mandibular protrusion means poor mandibular mobility. It predicts difficulty with jaw thrust and with displacing the tongue during laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: Why can even light sedation precipitate recurrent obstruction in untreated OSA?
options: Reduced pharyngeal dilator tone increases collapsibility of an already vulnerable upper airway
Sedatives primarily cause lower-airway bronchospasm in OSA
questions.explanation: Sedatives decrease upper airway muscle tone, which worsens collapse in patients with OSA.

questions.stem: Mallampati IV and limited mouth opening are present before planned EGD sedation. What must be established before administering sedatives?
options: A specific oxygenation/ventilation rescue and conversion-to-GA strategy
That the procedure is brief enough to ignore rescue difficulty
That minimal sedation will necessarily prevent airway obstruction
That every such patient receives awake intubation
questions.explanation: The lecture says develop a conversion plan before starting and plan rescue devices before medications. Airway findings shape the plan rather than automatically cancelling.

questions.stem: For cataract surgery with the face partially inaccessible under drapes, which finding most increases the consequence of sedation overshoot?
options: Mallampati III with limited neck extension
questions.explanation: Mallampati III and limited neck extension predict difficult rescue, made worse by limited access under the drapes.

questions.stem: A frail 89-year-old with EF 30% needs sedation. Which combination most directly increases risk?
options: Advanced age plus limited cardiopulmonary reserve
Neurologic loss of airway reflexes by definition
questions.explanation: Advanced age, frailty, and limited cardiopulmonary reserve increase sensitivity to sedatives and reduce tolerance of hypotension or hypoxemia.

questions.stem: Why is an airway assessment still necessary when only minimal oral sedation is planned?
options: Individual response is variable and sedation can unintentionally progress beyond the target level
Oral drugs always produce deep sedation
Airway assessment is required only for OSA
questions.explanation: The pre-sedation airway assessment is always performed, because any sedative can produce deeper sedation than intended.

questions.stem: Mallampati classification primarily estimates which anatomic relationship?
options: Oropharyngeal visibility relative to tongue/oral-cavity anatomy
questions.explanation: The Mallampati exam assesses oropharyngeal visibility, an indirect measure of tongue size relative to the oral cavity. This view is class III.

questions.stem: A healthy patient previously tolerated colonoscopy poorly despite adequate local/procedural technique. How should that history influence planning?
options: Anticipate greater analgesic/sedative requirements and the accompanying respiratory risk
Treat it as an absolute contraindication to sedation
questions.explanation: Poor tolerance suggests stimulation exceeds what light sedation covers. It predicts higher drug needs, which increases respiratory risk.

questions.stem: Which THREE caution factors apply to an obese EGD patient with severe OSA and active regurgitation? (Select 3)
questions.explanation: BMI 42, severe OSA, regurgitation when flat, and Mallampati IV map to obesity/difficult airway, OSA, and aspiration risk.

questions.stem: A patient with ankylosing spondylitis has almost no cervical flexion or extension. Which LEMON component is abnormal?
questions.explanation: Neck mobility assesses flexion and extension needed for the sniffing position and laryngoscopy.

questions.stem: A claustrophobic patient repeatedly cannot remain still for MRI despite preparation. How should this affect the anesthetic plan?
options: Recognize that required immobility and noncooperation may necessitate a deeper anesthetic plan with corresponding rescue/airway strategy
Classify this solely as a procedural issue unrelated to anesthetic depth
Keep sedation minimal regardless of movement
questions.explanation: Non-cooperative or unwilling patients need more caution, and procedures requiring immobility make cooperation essential. This often pushes the plan toward deeper sedation or GA with a protected airway.

questions.stem: An obese patient with OSA taking semaglutide reports ongoing nausea and early satiety before sedation. Which additional concern is most relevant?
options: Delayed gastric emptying with increased residual gastric-content/aspiration risk
questions.explanation: GLP-1 agonists delay gastric emptying, adding aspiration risk to his existing OSA and airway concerns.

questions.stem: Why is the supine position particularly relevant during MAC in untreated OSA?
options: It can worsen pharyngeal collapse and upper-airway obstruction
It improves functional residual capacity in obesity
questions.explanation: The lecture states supine increases airway obstruction, especially in obesity and OSA. Cataract surgery is done supine.

questions.stem: For a morbidly obese patient with OSA, which question should anchor the backup plan before MAC?
options: How will I rapidly oxygenate, ventilate, and secure the airway if sedation causes complete obstruction or apnea?
How quickly can I achieve deep sedation?
What is the maximum midazolam dose?
Can the proceduralist increase local anesthetic?
questions.explanation: Airway planning for sedation centers on rescue if sedation overshoots. In obesity and OSA, that means immediate means to ventilate and intubate.

questions.stem: Which FIVE findings belong in a routine pre-sedation airway examination? (Select 5)
questions.explanation: The pre-sedation airway exam includes mouth opening, dentition, Mallampati, mandibular mobility, neck range of motion, and thyromental distance. Peak flow is a pulmonary test, not part of the airway exam.

questions.stem: A patient with severe OSA previously had profound obstruction and desaturation during propofol sedation. Which strategy best reduces recurrence while still allowing titratable sedation?
options: Favor the least respiratory-depressing effective regimen, with careful titration and full rescue readiness
Use larger propofol boluses to shorten exposure
Combine propofol and opioid routinely because each dose can then be smaller
questions.explanation: Severe OSA with prior desaturation favors an agent with minimal respiratory depression. Synergistic combinations and larger boluses increase risk, and midazolam still depresses ventilation.

questions.stem: Why may remimazolam have more predictable offset than midazolam in substantial hepatic or renal dysfunction?
options: It is rapidly metabolized by nonspecific tissue esterases rather than relying primarily on hepatic/renal clearance
It cannot be antagonized by flumazenil
questions.explanation: Remimazolam is rapidly hydrolyzed mainly by tissue carboxylesterases to an inactive metabolite, so its offset is less dependent on hepatic CYP metabolism than midazolam. Severe organ dysfunction and patient factors can still alter clinical recovery; it can depress ventilation, provides little analgesia, and is antagonized by flumazenil.

questions.stem: Large tonsils and witnessed apneas most directly represent which LEMON category?
questions.explanation: Obstruction covers enlarged tonsils, oral pathology, sleep apnea, and tumors that can block the airway.

questions.stem: A frail 88-year-old with EF 30% requires sedation. Which dosing approach best matches the reduced physiologic reserve?
options: Use smaller incremental doses with slower titration and close reassessment
Give one large bolus to shorten exposure
Avoid all sedation solely because of age
questions.explanation: Age and limited cardiac reserve strongly increase drug effect and slow circulation time. Small, slowly titrated doses with close monitoring are safer than standard or bolus dosing.

questions.stem: A patient with severe pulmonary hypertension and COPD undergoes TEE under MAC. Which sedation complication is particularly dangerous because it can raise pulmonary vascular resistance and precipitate RV failure?
options: Hypoxemia and hypercapnia from hypoventilation/airway obstruction
questions.explanation: Pulmonary hypertension is a key risk condition in MAC preop assessment. Hypoxemia and hypercarbia from oversedation raise PVR and can precipitate right heart failure.

questions.stem: Which combination most strongly predicts difficult bag-mask rescue?
options: Full neck extension in a thin patient
questions.explanation: Facial hair prevents a mask seal and OSA predicts obstruction, both predictors of difficult BMV. The other findings are reassuring.

questions.stem: Before selecting sedatives for a procedure, which procedural characteristic most directly determines whether analgesic supplementation will be needed?
options: Expected intensity and duration of noxious stimulation
questions.explanation: Estimating the analgesic requirement from the expected stimulus drives drug choice and planned depth. A liver ablation needs far more analgesia than a skin biopsy.

questions.stem: A patient must follow neurologic commands during carotid stenting. Which preoperative factor is essential to verify before choosing MAC?
options: Ability to understand and cooperate with intraoperative neurologic testing
questions.explanation: Ability to cooperate is part of the preop assessment, and procedures needing patient cooperation or neurologic checks depend on it. If he cannot cooperate, the plan may need to change.

questions.stem: Why is a prolonged supine MAC especially risky in morbid obesity?
options: Obesity/supine positioning promotes obstruction while prolonged exposure increases cumulative sedation and unsecured-airway risk
questions.explanation: Supine increases obstruction in obesity, and long procedures add exposure to an unsecured airway and restless, deeper-than-intended sedation.

questions.stem: Which EGD patient most strongly favors a secured airway rather than routine MAC?
options: A patient with active regurgitation, severe OSA, and a predicted difficult rescue airway
A patient with controlled hypertension and mild anxiety
A healthy young adult with dyspepsia
A patient with stable mild asthma
questions.explanation: Active regurgitation with a difficult airway and OSA combines high aspiration risk with difficult rescue. A protected airway is safer.

questions.stem: Why can a standard propofol bolus produce disproportionately severe apnea and hypotension in an older frail adult?
options: Greater pharmacodynamic sensitivity and reduced cardiopulmonary reserve make a given dose less tolerable
Older adults metabolize propofol much faster
Advanced age alone causes difficult mask ventilation
questions.explanation: Age reduces cardiopulmonary reserve and increases drug sensitivity, so the same dose produces larger effects that are less well tolerated.

questions.stem: A patient on chronic oxycodone is scheduled for colonoscopy. Which approach best accounts for both tolerance and synergistic respiratory depression?
options: Expect altered analgesic requirements but titrate all sedative/opioid combinations carefully to effect
Dose exactly as for an opioid-naive patient
Avoid monitoring because opioid tolerance protects ventilation
questions.explanation: Chronic opioid use produces tolerance and unpredictable responses. Expect different requirements, titrate carefully, and watch for exaggerated respiratory depression when drugs are combined.

questions.stem: The rescue airway cart is stored down the hallway from the procedure room. Why is this unsafe even for planned moderate sedation?
options: Unintended progression can occur rapidly, so rescue equipment must be immediately available before sedation begins
Advanced airway equipment is needed only for planned deep sedation
Rescue equipment is necessary only with known OSA
Equipment can safely be retrieved after desaturation begins
questions.explanation: Airway rescue equipment must be immediately available before sedation begins, since depth can change without warning.

questions.stem: Mallampati II, good mouth opening, and full neck motion are present, but thyromental distance is markedly short. Which finding should most alter rescue planning?
questions.explanation: A short thyromental distance suggests a small mandibular space and an anterior larynx, predicting a poor view despite otherwise reassuring findings.

questions.stem: An anxious cataract patient has OSA and a potentially difficult airway that will be partly inaccessible under surgical drapes. Which plan best balances comfort with rescue risk?
options: Use explanation/reassurance and carefully titrated light anxiolysis while preserving responsiveness and ventilation
Plan deep sedation so the patient cannot move
Give repeated opioid/benzodiazepine boluses until asleep
Ignore airway access because cataract surgery is brief
questions.explanation: Anxiety is managed with expectation setting and careful anxiolysis. With Mallampati III, OSA, and limited airway access under drapes, deep sedation adds real risk.

questions.stem: A patient reports a prior difficult intubation but does not know the details. What is the most useful next step before sedation?
options: Clarify the prior event and obtain available airway records so the rescue plan reflects what actually worked or failed
Proceed unchanged because intubation is not planned
Deepen sedation to reduce anxiety about the prior event
questions.explanation: Prior difficult intubation is a key history item. Details guide the rescue plan in case sedation becomes deeper than intended.

questions.stem: An anesthesia professional is providing MAC. Which general monitoring principle applies regardless of whether the patient currently appears only lightly sedated?
options: Standard anesthesia monitoring appropriate to MAC remains in place because the anesthetic can deepen and intervention may be required
Pulse oximetry alone is sufficient until deep sedation occurs
Monitoring is determined solely by the proceduralist
ECG is unnecessary in healthy patients receiving MAC
questions.explanation: The lecture states that if an anesthesia provider is involved, all ASA monitors must be applied, regardless of the planned depth.

questions.stem: During MAC, how should noninvasive blood pressure monitoring be scheduled when no arterial catheter is indicated?
options: At frequent regular intervals consistent with anesthesia monitoring standards and more often when clinically indicated
Only before and after the procedure
questions.explanation: During anesthesia care, arterial blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every 5 minutes under ASA basic monitoring standards, with more frequent measurement when the patient's condition or anesthetic warrants it. A universal 3-minute MAC interval should not be taught as the standard.

questions.stem: Sedation unexpectedly progresses to general anesthesia/TIVA with hemodynamic instability. How should blood-pressure monitoring change?
options: Increase measurement frequency beyond the routine interval as needed to manage the instability
Decrease frequency because the patient is immobile
Stop NIBP if pulse oximetry is normal
Use a fixed 3-minute interval as the only acceptable response
questions.explanation: ASA basic monitoring requires arterial blood pressure and heart rate assessment at least every 5 minutes during anesthesia, but unstable physiology may require more frequent noninvasive measurements or invasive monitoring. The response should be driven by clinical need rather than a universal 3-minute rule.

questions.stem: A healthy patient receives non-anesthesia procedural sedation, while another receives MAC from an anesthesia professional. Which statement best distinguishes monitoring expectations?
options: MAC follows anesthesia monitoring standards throughout; non-anesthesia procedural-sedation monitoring follows the applicable sedation standard and patient risk
Neither requires ECG or blood-pressure monitoring
Both require identical monitoring solely because IV sedatives are used
MAC requires less monitoring because an anesthesia professional is present
questions.explanation: During MAC the ECG is continuously displayed regardless of depth. During nurse-administered procedural sedation, ECG use is based on depth and patient risk, so a healthy patient at moderate depth may not need it.

questions.stem: Which pair should be continuously observed during procedural sedation/MAC because oxygenation can remain normal briefly despite deteriorating ventilation?
options: Pulse oximetry plus ventilation monitoring such as capnography
questions.explanation: Oxygenation and ventilation are distinct. Pulse oximetry continuously tracks oxygen saturation, while capnography or another appropriate ventilation monitor can identify hypoventilation or apnea before oxygen saturation falls, particularly when supplemental oxygen is used.

questions.stem: A MAC case converts to TIVA/general anesthesia after regional anesthesia fails. Which monitoring domain should now be actively managed to prevent clinically significant unintended temperature change?
options: Central venous pressure in every case
questions.explanation: During general anesthesia, temperature should be measured when clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected. It is not accurate to teach that continuous core-temperature measurement is mandatory for every TIVA/GA case.

questions.stem: SpO2 remains 99% on supplemental oxygen while RR falls to 5/min and ETCO2 rises. Why is capnography more informative at this moment?
options: Supplemental oxygen can delay desaturation despite worsening hypoventilation
Pulse oximetry cannot measure oxygenation during sedation
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen delays desaturation, so SpO2 can stay normal while ventilation fails. Capnography detects hypoventilation and apnea first.

questions.stem: During propofol MAC on supplemental oxygen, apnea goes unnoticed until profound desaturation occurs. Which monitor would most likely have provided the earliest warning?
options: Continuous capnography from an appropriate sampling interface
questions.explanation: A sampling cannula detects hypoventilation and apnea immediately. More oxygen delays desaturation further, and SpO2 tones and BP cycling detect the problem late.

questions.stem: A sedated patient has regular capnogram waveforms with a zero baseline and stable ETCO2 near 40 mmHg. Which conclusion is best supported by the tracing?
options: Exhaled ventilation appears regular and adequate at that moment
questions.explanation: A regular exhaled CO2 waveform with a stable trend supports ongoing exhaled ventilation at that moment. A nasal or mask ETCO2 value does not by itself prove normal PaCO2, define sedation depth, exclude aspiration risk, or confirm intact airway reflexes.

questions.stem: During propofol-opioid sedation, respiratory rate progressively slows and ETCO2 rises while SpO2 remains 97% on oxygen. What is the best interpretation?
options: Progressive hypoventilation masked by supplemental oxygen
Adequate ventilation because oxygen saturation remains normal
A normal response to procedural stimulation
questions.explanation: Slowing rate and rising ETCO2 after propofol plus fentanyl indicate hypoventilation. Supplemental O2 keeps SpO2 normal, which is why SpO2 lags.

questions.stem: Bradypnea and rising ETCO2 develop after a sedative bolus while SpO2 remains normal on oxygen. What is the first response?
options: Hold further sedative, stimulate/open the airway, and support ventilation as needed
Increase oxygen flow and continue the same sedative rate
Give another sedative bolus to prevent movement
Wait for SpO2 to fall before intervening
questions.explanation: Bradypnea with rising ETCO2 is hypoventilation. Stimulate, support the airway, and stop adding drug; normal SpO2 on oxygen is falsely reassuring.

questions.stem: The capnogram abruptly becomes flat during sedation while SpO2 remains 99% on oxygen. What should be done first?
options: Assess the patient immediately for apnea or obstruction while checking the sampling system
Assume artifact because SpO2 is normal
Wait for the next blood-pressure cycle
questions.explanation: Loss of the capnogram is apnea, obstruction, or disconnection until proven otherwise. SpO2 lags, so assess the patient before attributing it to artifact.

questions.stem: Why can an apneic, deeply sedated patient remain at SpO2 99% for a period while receiving supplemental oxygen?
options: Increased alveolar oxygen reserve delays desaturation despite absent ventilation
questions.explanation: Preoxygenation and supplemental O2 fill alveoli and blood with oxygen, so saturation falls only after reserve is used. ETCO2 changes immediately.

questions.stem: If apnea begins while a patient receives supplemental oxygen and only pulse oximetry is used to detect respiratory failure, what is the key limitation?
options: Desaturation may be delayed for minutes after ventilation stops
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen fills the FRC, so SpO2 stays normal for minutes after apnea. Capnography shows apnea immediately.

questions.stem: A sedation adverse event occurs even though ECG, oxygenation, and capnography monitors are connected. Which failure can still allow apnea to progress unnoticed?
options: Failure to maintain continuous vigilance and respond to monitor changes
questions.explanation: Monitoring included ECG, inspired O2, and end-tidal CO2. The failure was not attending to the monitors, not a lack of them.

questions.stem: What is the central safety lesson when appropriate monitors are applied but respiratory arrest still goes unrecognized?
options: Monitoring is protective only when data are continuously observed, interpreted, and acted upon
Adding more monitors eliminates the need for vigilance
The proceduralist should assume responsibility for anesthesia monitoring
questions.explanation: Case 1 shows that applied monitors do not protect the patient without continuous attention and action.

questions.stem: A patient receives sedative medication in holding and arrests during transport to the procedure room. Which systems error is most important?
options: Sedation was followed by transport without appropriate ongoing monitoring and airway-rescue readiness
The patient was not intubated before every sedative dose
Too much supplemental oxygen was used
Transport should never occur after any anxiolytic
questions.explanation: Once sedation is given, monitoring and airway readiness must continue during transport.

questions.stem: Why might invasive or advanced hemodynamic monitoring be appropriate for TAVR under MAC but unnecessary for a healthy patient having a superficial biopsy?
options: Monitoring intensity should reflect patient physiology and procedural risk
Advanced monitoring is mandatory for every MAC
Advanced monitoring is limited to inhaled general anesthesia
Monitoring is based solely on proceduralist preference
questions.explanation: Advanced hemodynamic monitoring during sedation and MAC depends on patient condition and procedure complexity. The TAVR patient likely needs it; the biopsy patient does not.

questions.stem: Which THREE variables are continuously monitored during anesthesia-provider MAC? (Select 3)
options: Invasive arterial pressure in every case
questions.explanation: During MAC, heart rate, SpO2, and ECG are continuous, along with ventilation. Temperature is used when indicated, and invasive or advanced monitoring depends on the patient.

questions.stem: A 3-hour burn procedure under MAC has continuous ECG and SpO2 but no ventilation or temperature monitoring. Which omissions are most important?
options: Capnography/ventilation monitoring plus temperature monitoring because the prolonged exposed case makes temperature clinically relevant
Processed EEG plus invasive arterial pressure
Urine output plus a second ECG lead
None because SpO2 substitutes for ventilation
questions.explanation: MAC requires monitoring of oxygenation, ventilation, circulation, and temperature when indicated. A long burn case in a cool room indicates temperature monitoring, and capnography was absent.

questions.stem: During sedation, ETCO2 rises from 38 to 58 mmHg while SpO2 remains 98% on oxygen. What does the trend indicate?
options: Alveolar ventilation is worsening before oxygenation has failed
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 means hypoventilation. On supplemental oxygen, SpO2 stays normal until reserves are exhausted.

questions.stem: A spontaneously breathing patient has nasal-cannula ETCO2 28 mmHg while PaCO2 is 44 mmHg. How should the cannula value be interpreted?
options: Use waveform and trend; dilution by oxygen/room air can make the absolute ETCO2 underestimate PaCO2
Discard capnography whenever it differs from PaCO2
Use pulse oximetry as a substitute for ventilation monitoring
questions.explanation: Nasal cannula sampling mixes exhaled gas with oxygen and room air, so values read low. The waveform and trend still reflect ventilation.

questions.stem: The capnogram disappears, but the patient is awake, speaking clearly, and visibly breathing. What should be checked first?
options: Sampling interface/line position and mouth breathing
questions.explanation: A talking patient is breathing. A lost waveform is then likely technical or due to mouth breathing, but you still verify at the bedside.

questions.stem: Why is pulse oximetry alone inadequate for ventilation monitoring during moderate sedation with supplemental oxygen?
options: It measures oxygenation and may remain normal despite substantial hypoventilation
It detects apnea earlier than capnography
It measures ventilation only when oxygen is not administered
questions.explanation: SpO2 measures oxygenation and lags, especially on oxygen. Capnography detects hypoventilation and apnea directly.

questions.stem: A review of sedation adverse events shows obstruction, hypoventilation, and aspiration predominate. Which design priority follows most directly?
options: Airway/ventilation surveillance and rapid rescue capability should be central to the sedation safety plan
Cardiovascular monitoring can replace respiratory monitoring
Medication reconciliation is the only meaningful prevention strategy
Respiratory rescue equipment is unnecessary when capnography is used
questions.explanation: Hypoventilation, obstruction, and aspiration account for 28 of 40 events, consistent with respiratory events being a major source of adverse sedation outcomes.

questions.stem: SpO2 begins falling only after the ETCO2 waveform has already disappeared during sedation on supplemental oxygen. What does this sequence imply?
options: Ventilation failed earlier, and oxygen reserve temporarily delayed recognition by pulse oximetry
questions.explanation: By the time SpO2 falls on supplemental O2, apnea or obstruction has usually been present for some time. Treat urgently.

questions.stem: During sedation, complete laryngospasm abruptly stops airflow. Which standard monitor should reflect the loss of ventilation first?
questions.explanation: Capnography loses its waveform as soon as airflow stops; SpO2 lags and ECG and BP changes come later.

questions.stem: The proceduralist asks to remove capnography during moderate sedation because the cannula is uncomfortable. What is the best response?
options: Modify/reposition the interface while maintaining required ventilation monitoring
Remove it if SpO2 remains above 95%
Replace it with visual chest observation alone
Increase oxygen flow and stop CO2 monitoring
questions.explanation: Capnography is required during moderate and deep sedation. Reposition or change the cannula, but keep monitoring ventilation.

questions.stem: During moderate/deep procedural sedation, blood pressure is checked only every 15 minutes despite ongoing IV sedative administration. What is the problem?
options: The interval is too long for routine moderate/deep sedation monitoring
Fifteen-minute measurements are sufficient whenever initial BP is normal
Only invasive arterial pressure is acceptable
Blood pressure need not be monitored during sedation
questions.explanation: BP should be measured at least every 5 minutes during moderate and deep procedural sedation. Stable vitals do not lengthen the interval.

questions.stem: Two sedated patients both have ETCO2 58 mmHg; one is bradypneic and the other has rapid shallow breathing. What common physiologic problem can produce both patterns?
questions.explanation: ETCO2 in a spontaneously breathing patient reflects alveolar ventilation. Bradypnea and rapid shallow breathing can both leave alveolar ventilation inadequate.

questions.stem: A deeply sedated patient receiving nasal oxygen becomes apneic. Which sequence is expected?
options: The capnogram changes immediately; SpO2 may remain normal temporarily
SpO2 falls before the capnogram changes
ETCO2 remains normal until desaturation occurs
questions.explanation: The capnogram flattens at the onset of apnea while SpO2 holds for minutes on supplemental oxygen. That lag is why capnography is central during sedation.

questions.stem: Which TWO bedside measures most directly assess ventilation during spontaneous-breathing sedation? (Select 2)
questions.explanation: Capnography and respiratory rate and depth assess ventilation directly. SpO2 lags on supplemental oxygen, and BP, temperature, and HR do not measure breathing.

questions.stem: During MAC, ETCO2 rises and respiratory rate slows after propofol plus opioid administration while SpO2 remains normal. Which mechanism is most likely?
options: CO2-absorbent exhaustion in a nonrebreathing nasal-cannula setup
questions.explanation: Rising ETCO2 with slow breathing after sedatives and opioids indicates cumulative respiratory depression. The synergy is emphasized in the lecture.

questions.stem: A MAC case converts to TIVA/general anesthesia. Which monitoring consideration becomes especially important as anesthetic depth, duration, and heat loss increase?
options: Assess and monitor temperature when clinically significant change is intended, anticipated, or suspected
questions.explanation: General anesthesia increases the importance of thermal management, but ASA standards do not require continuous temperature measurement in every case. Temperature is measured when clinically significant changes are intended, anticipated, or suspected; oxygenation and circulation monitoring continue.

questions.stem: A 70-year-old with CAD undergoes deep sedation for cardioversion. Why is continuous ECG particularly appropriate?
options: Both the depth of sedation and cardiovascular comorbidity increase the importance of rhythm/ischemia surveillance
ECG replaces pulse oximetry during deep sedation
ECG is unnecessary if capnography is present
Cardioversion eliminates arrhythmia risk after the shock
questions.explanation: For procedural sedation, ECG use is based on depth and risk and is routinely used for deeper sedation. This patient needs it for both reasons.

questions.stem: A patient with stable COPD has baseline ETCO2 around 50 mmHg. During MAC, what is most useful for detecting respiratory deterioration?
options: A change in waveform and ETCO2 trend from the patient's baseline
Whether ETCO2 is above 40 mmHg at any point
A single end-tidal value after the procedure
questions.explanation: Some patients have chronically elevated CO2. The trend and waveform are more useful than a single absolute number.

questions.stem: Which THREE statements about pulse oximetry during sedation are correct? (Select 3)
options: Supplemental oxygen can delay its response to hypoventilation
It does not directly measure ventilation
It is unnecessary during moderate sedation
questions.explanation: Pulse oximetry is continuous in every setting and reflects oxygenation. On oxygen it lags hypoventilation, so it cannot replace capnography.

questions.stem: During MAC, conversation in the room distracts the anesthesia provider while the capnogram deteriorates. Which safety principle is most directly violated?
options: Continuous vigilance must be maintained despite environmental distraction
Capnography is unnecessary if the patient appears asleep
The proceduralist should monitor ventilation instead
questions.explanation: Case 1 showed that conversation with the gastroenterologist led to loss of situational awareness and unrecognized apnea.

questions.stem: During TIVA/general anesthesia, noninvasive BP cycling is left at a longer interval than the institution's anesthesia standard despite active hemodynamic changes. What should be done?
options: Increase measurement frequency to meet the applicable anesthesia standard and clinical condition
Keep the longer interval because TIVA stabilizes BP
Stop NIBP if ECG is normal
Measure BP only after drug boluses
questions.explanation: During anesthesia, arterial blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every 5 minutes under ASA basic monitoring standards. Active hemodynamic change may justify substantially more frequent measurements or invasive monitoring, but a universal 3-minute requirement for TIVA/GA is not the ASA standard.

questions.stem: ECG leads are removed during MAC and not replaced for 15 minutes. Which principle is violated?
options: Continuous ECG surveillance during anesthesia-provider MAC
ECG is required only at induction and emergence
ECG is required only when SpO2 falls
questions.explanation: MAC requires the ECG to be continuously displayed for the entire case. Pulse oximetry and NIBP cannot detect arrhythmias like VT.

questions.stem: After a sedative bolus, which monitor usually provides the earliest objective evidence of respiratory depression?
questions.explanation: Capnography reflects each breath, so changes in rate and pattern appear first. SpO2, HR, and BP change later.

questions.stem: Which MAC case most clearly makes temperature monitoring clinically important?
options: A prolonged burn procedure with large exposed surface area
No MAC case ever requires temperature monitoring
questions.explanation: Temperature monitoring during MAC is required when clinically indicated, such as long cases with large exposed surface areas. It is continuous under TIVA/GA.

questions.stem: Which FOUR factors should guide sedative titration when the patient becomes too deep during low stimulation and too light during painful moments? (Select 4)
questions.explanation: Titration should account for kinetics, effect-site delay, drug interactions, and changing stimulus. Matching depth to the stimulus prevents both overshoot and undershoot.

questions.stem: Two propofol boluses are given in rapid succession before the first has reached peak clinical effect; apnea follows. Which error occurred?
options: Dose stacking across the effect-site delay
questions.explanation: Effect-site delay means the first bolus had not peaked when the second was given, so their effects combined.

questions.stem: A moderately sedated patient has RR 12/min, regular capnogram morphology, and stable ETCO2 45 mmHg without a concerning trend. What is the best response?
options: Continue close observation rather than treating a single mildly elevated stable value
Increase sedation because ETCO2 is above 40
questions.explanation: A regular waveform and normal rate with a stable ETCO2 in the mid 40s is acceptable. The trend matters more than one mildly elevated value.

questions.stem: When an anesthesia professional provides MAC, what overarching monitoring principle applies even if the patient currently appears minimally sedated?
options: Standard anesthesia monitoring remains appropriate because depth and physiologic risk can change
Monitoring can be reduced to pulse oximetry
Monitoring depends only on ASA physical status
Monitors can be removed after initial stability
questions.explanation: The lecture states that if an anesthesia provider is involved, all ASA monitors must be applied.

questions.stem: The nasal capnogram intermittently disappears whenever a sedated patient breathes through the mouth, while chest excursion and oxygenation remain stable. What is the likely explanation?
options: The nasal sampling interface is missing exhaled gas during mouth breathing
questions.explanation: Nasal sampling captures exhaled gas from the nose, so mouth breathing can make the waveform disappear despite normal ventilation.

questions.stem: During deep sedation, BP is measured only every 15 minutes and significant hypotension is discovered late. Which process error contributed?
options: Use of noninvasive rather than invasive pressure
questions.explanation: A 15-minute blood-pressure interval can delay recognition of important hypotension. During anesthesia care, blood pressure and heart rate are evaluated at least every 5 minutes, with greater frequency when clinically indicated.

questions.stem: What common systems failure can link sedation injuries even when the necessary monitors are physically available?
options: Failure to maintain or attend to continuous monitoring after sedative administration
Monitoring equipment itself is inherently unreliable
Alarms eliminate the need for direct observation
questions.explanation: Both cases show that harm follows lapses in attention or monitoring after sedation, not equipment failure.

questions.stem: During sedation, the patient snores and the capnogram becomes low-amplitude and irregular rather than disappearing completely. Which problem is most likely?
questions.explanation: Snoring with small, irregular waveforms suggests partial obstruction. Jaw thrust or repositioning is often the fix.

questions.stem: Which FOUR resources should be immediately available where anesthesia-provider MAC is performed? (Select 4)
options: A volatile vaporizer in every location
questions.explanation: The MAC environment requires oxygen, suction, ventilation equipment, emergency drugs, capnography, and advanced airway equipment.

questions.stem: Minimal sedation is intended, but an anesthesia professional is providing MAC. Which monitoring approach is most appropriate?
options: Use standard anesthesia monitoring rather than reducing monitoring solely because current depth is light
Delay ECG/NIBP until moderate sedation develops
Monitor only when the patient stops responding normally
questions.explanation: The procedural sedation BP interval (at least every 5 minutes) is written for moderate and deep sedation. When an anesthesia provider is involved, standard ASA monitoring still applies.

questions.stem: RR falls to 6/min and ETCO2 rises while SpO2 remains 96% on oxygen. Why should intervention occur before desaturation?
options: Ventilatory failure is already present, and oxygen supplementation can mask it until reserve is exhausted
SpO2 96% proves hypoxemia is imminent within seconds
questions.explanation: Once oxygen reserve is depleted, desaturation and arrest can follow rapidly, so early intervention matters.

questions.stem: A sedated patient receives oxygen by face mask. Which approach best assesses ventilation continuously?
options: Use an interface that samples exhaled CO2 while oxygen is delivered
questions.explanation: Capnography sampled at the mask gives a waveform and trend of ventilation; SpO2 lags and fogging is not quantitative.

questions.stem: ETCO2 abruptly reads zero with an intact-appearing sampling line while pulse and SpO2 remain normal. What is the first action?
options: Assess the patient for airflow and open/support the airway while verifying the sampling system
Replace the capnography module before touching the patient
Recalibrate the monitor before bedside assessment
questions.explanation: With intact sampling, an ETCO2 of 0 means no exhaled gas. Check for apnea or obstruction immediately; SpO2 can remain normal for minutes.

questions.stem: Why can pulse oximetry provide a dangerously late warning of respiratory depression during sedation with supplemental oxygen?
options: Oxygenation may remain acceptable for a period despite worsening hypoventilation or apnea
Probe processing always delays SpO2 by several minutes
SpO2 is completely unaffected by apnea
Pulse oximetry measures ventilation rather than oxygenation
questions.explanation: Supplemental oxygen delays desaturation, so hypoventilation may be advanced before SpO2 drops.

questions.stem: A brief intensely painful biopsy and a long minimally stimulating endoscopy are planned. Which feature most directly determines the peak analgesic/sedative requirement?
options: Intensity and variability of noxious stimulation
questions.explanation: Procedure selection weighs the intensity and variability of stimulation, duration, position and airway access, ability to interrupt, bleeding or aspiration risk, and the need for cooperation.

questions.stem: Why does a procedure that cannot be rapidly paused for airway rescue make deep sedation with an unsecured airway less attractive?
options: Airway deterioration may occur while procedural access prevents immediate rescue
Interrupting a procedure increases infection risk
Longer procedures always require general anesthesia
Sedation cannot be used outside the operating room
questions.explanation: If a procedure cannot be paused for airway rescue, the risk of an unsecured airway is higher and GA may be safer.

questions.stem: Which procedure is generally most compatible with sedation when patient and procedural factors are otherwise favorable?
options: Cemented total hip arthroplasty without regional anesthesia
questions.explanation: Sedation suits procedures like colonoscopy, EGD, flexible sigmoidoscopy, biopsies, reductions, and short cardiac procedures. The others need GA or neuraxial anesthesia.

questions.stem: Which cardiovascular procedure often requires a brief period of deep sedation because the stimulus is intense but extremely short?
options: Pacemaker generator change under effective local anesthesia
questions.explanation: Cardioversion lasts seconds but is intensely stimulating, so brief deep sedation is typical. Angiograms and generator changes are usually done under lighter sedation with local.

questions.stem: Why does upper endoscopy generally create more difficult airway rescue than colonoscopy at the same sedation depth?
options: The endoscope shares the oropharyngeal airway and can impede access during rescue
Upper endoscopy is always more painful
questions.explanation: During EGD, the scope occupies the pharynx, so airway access and rescue are harder.

questions.stem: During awake craniotomy, which procedural requirement most constrains sedative depth?
options: The patient must remain able to cooperate with neurologic testing
questions.explanation: Awake craniotomy requires the patient to cooperate with neurologic testing, which limits how deep sedation can go.

questions.stem: Which TWO MRI characteristics most increase anesthetic risk during sedation? (Select 2)
options: Restricted physical access to the airway/patient in the scanner environment
questions.explanation: An MRI requires long immobility and limits airway access, which makes interrupting for rescue harder. Stimulation is minimal, and bleeding and gastric issues are not the main concerns.

questions.stem: A laterally positioned sedated patient develops worsening oxygenation. Which change can contribute?
options: Compression of the dependent lung can reduce its compliance and FRC
The dependent lung always gains FRC
Lateral positioning guarantees improved V/Q matching
questions.explanation: Lateral positioning decreases compliance and FRC in the dependent lung, worsening oxygenation.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, systemic hypotension develops. Which positioning-related consequence is most concerning?
options: Cerebral perfusion pressure at the brain may be substantially lower than the arm-cuff pressure suggests
Dependent-lung FRC always falls to zero
Upper-airway obstruction is eliminated by the upright position
questions.explanation: In the beach-chair position, hydrostatic height differences mean pressure at brain level may be lower than a cuff measured on the arm unless the gradient is accounted for. Hypotension can therefore threaten cerebral perfusion; the issue is not that upright positioning itself simply 'alters autoregulation.'

questions.stem: During a prolonged prone operation, which combination most increases postoperative visual-loss risk?
options: Major blood loss/anemia with prolonged prone positioning
Short duration with minimal blood loss
Normal hemoglobin and neutral head position
questions.explanation: POVL risk factors include prolonged surgery, substantial blood loss, anemia, obesity, and vascular disease.

questions.stem: Which THREE measures help reduce postoperative visual-loss risk in prolonged prone surgery? (Select 3)
options: Avoid direct external pressure on the eyes
Keep the head neutral and, when feasible, level with or above the heart
Deliberately position the head below the heart
Accept profound anemia to reduce transfusion
questions.explanation: POVL prevention includes avoiding eye pressure, keeping perfusion and oxygenation adequate, and keeping the head neutral and level or above the heart.

questions.stem: Why is prolonged prone deep sedation with an unsecured airway especially hazardous?
options: Airway access is restricted and airway/facial edema can make rescue progressively harder
Prone positioning guarantees improved airway patency
Every prone procedure automatically requires neuromuscular blockade
questions.explanation: Prone positioning limits airway access for rescue and can cause airway and facial edema.

questions.stem: A morbidly obese patient with severe OSA is sedated supine. Which airway change should be anticipated?
options: Loss of pharyngeal tone can markedly worsen upper-airway obstruction
questions.explanation: Supine positioning worsens airway obstruction, especially with obesity and OSA. Consider ramping or a lateral position when possible.

questions.stem: Why can a 4-hour MAC create more airway risk than a 20-minute MAC in an otherwise similar patient?
options: Longer unsecured-airway exposure and cumulative drug/stimulation changes increase opportunities for deterioration
Longer cases require less total sedative
Restlessness becomes less likely with time
Monitoring can be reduced after the first hour
questions.explanation: Long procedures extend the time with an unsecured airway and increase the chance of oversedation from restlessness.

questions.stem: A patient must follow commands during carotid stenting. How should this requirement influence sedation?
options: Preserve sufficient responsiveness for reliable neurologic testing
Use neuromuscular blockade to prevent movement
questions.explanation: Procedures requiring cooperation or neurologic testing limit depth, since the patient must respond.

questions.stem: During facial surgery under MAC, supplemental oxygen accumulates beneath drapes near electrocautery. Which hazard becomes a major anesthetic concern?
options: Operating-room fire in an oxygen-enriched field
Local anesthetic systemic toxicity by definition
questions.explanation: Fire risk is highest when oxygen collects under drapes near an ignition source during head and neck procedures.

questions.stem: TEE and synchronized cardioversion are examples of what procedural group commonly managed with carefully selected sedation techniques?
questions.explanation: TEE, selected cardiac catheterizations, and cardioversion are short cardiovascular procedures often done under sedation when appropriate.

questions.stem: A patient with severe COPD, predicted difficult airway, and esophageal food impaction is scheduled for EGD. Which principle should determine MAC versus a secured airway?
options: Integrate aspiration risk, airway rescue difficulty, comorbidity, and procedural requirements rather than relying on the usual anesthetic for EGD
Use MAC because EGD is usually performed under sedation
Choose solely according to patient preference
questions.explanation: A procedure that is usually done under sedation is appropriate only when the airway, comorbidities, complexity, and stimulation allow it. This patient may need GA with a protected airway.

questions.stem: A percutaneous biopsy carries meaningful hemorrhage risk. How should that risk affect sedation planning?
options: Ensure monitoring/access and a plan for sudden hemodynamic deterioration or escalation of care
It eliminates the need for airway planning
It guarantees general anesthesia is unnecessary
questions.explanation: Bleeding risk means sudden hemodynamic changes may occur, which shapes monitoring and readiness to convert.

questions.stem: Why is shoulder-dislocation reduction often well suited to brief deep sedation in an appropriately selected patient?
options: The stimulus is intense but short, and rapid recovery is desirable
The patient must follow commands throughout reduction
questions.explanation: Joint reductions are short and intensely stimulating, and patients need to recover quickly afterward.

questions.stem: During beach-chair MAC, arm BP falls to 85/50 mmHg. Which concern should drive prompt reassessment and treatment?
